contract_plain_english: For a differentiable state q and differentiable flux f, the spatial derivative of the composite flux is its Jacobian times the spatial derivative of the state. Thus q_t + partial_x(f(q)) = 0 is the same classical equation as q_t + f'(q) q_x = 0.

binders: A state q(x,t) with values in R^m on a one-dimensional space-time domain.
A differentiable flux f: R^m -> R^m.
The spatial coordinate x and time coordinate t.
conclusions: The chain rule gives partial_x(f(q(x,t))) = Df(q(x,t)) q_x(x,t).
Consequently the conservation law can be rewritten pointwise as q_t + f'(q) q_x = 0, where f'(q) is the flux Jacobian matrix.
definitions_and_conventions: f'(q) denotes the Jacobian derivative Df(q); for m components it is an m by m matrix.
q_x is the spatial derivative vector and f'(q) q_x is matrix-vector multiplication.
Subscripts t and x denote partial derivatives.
'Quasilinear form' means that the highest-order derivatives q_t and q_x occur linearly, with a coefficient f'(q) that may depend on q.
hypotheses: q and f are differentiable enough for the spatial chain rule to apply to f(q(x,t)).
The differential conservation law q_t(x,t) + partial_x(f(q(x,t))) = 0 is under consideration.
implicit_context: The selected equation is one-dimensional and homogeneous, with no source term.
The formula covers the scalar case m = 1 as well as systems.
The subsequent hyperbolicity discussion treats f'(q) as the state-dependent analogue of the constant matrix A.

details: Equation (1.9) is presented as a rewriting of equation (1.8), not as an additional dynamical assumption.
The equivalence is classical and depends on differentiability of q and f.
For vector q, f'(q) is a Jacobian matrix acting on q_x.
The source does not restrict f to be linear in this task.
The text says the quasilinear form suggests hyperbolicity when f'(q) satisfies the earlier spectral conditions for A; this is contextual motivation rather than part of the chain-rule identity itself.

undebatable_constraints: The coefficient multiplying q_x is the derivative/Jacobian f'(q), evaluated at the current state q.
In the system case, f'(q) q_x is matrix-vector multiplication with matching dimension m.
The rewrite must retain the sign and zero right-hand side: q_t + f'(q) q_x = 0.
The claim is a smooth chain-rule rewrite of partial_x(f(q)), not a claim that f is linear or that f'(q) is constant.
No eigenvalue condition is needed merely to establish the rewrite.
